newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul warns Internet providers on North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Seoul warns Internet providers on North Korea.

text.p: Worried about North Korea's reported entry into cyberspace, South Korean authorities on Wednesday warned Internet providers they risked lengthy jail terms by distributing Pyongyang propaganda.
The warning followed a report by South Korea's Yonhap news agency that Pyongyang's Korea Central News Agency (KCNA) will open a site on the World Wide Web on Thursday to mark its 50th anniversary.
There has been no announcement by KCNA, but Seoul prosecutors are moving swiftly to ensure that KCNA dispatches -- the voice of North Korea's Stalinist leadership -- do not circulate in South Korea.
"We still don't know what information KCNA will carry," one prosecution official said.
"But if any anti-South Korean propaganda is sent out by a local Internet user, it will violate laws banning such activities and therefore be punished."
South Korea bans distribution of any information or material benefiting North Korea and violators can be jailed for up to seven years.
KCNA stories are a fairly reliable barometer of inter-Korean relations, and lately they have been filled with biting invective against President Kim Young-sam.

On Monday, for example, KCNA carried an item from an official North Korean newspaper describing Kim and the South Korean leadership as "heinous gangsters" and "fascist tyrants" for their crackdown on a pro-Pyongyang student group.
"They are not qualified to live in this world," KCNA reported.
The prosecution official denied domestic media reports that authorities have asked Internet providers to block access to North Korea's Internet site.
"Blocking access to Internet sites is difficult and could have serious side effects," he said.

South Korea earlier this year blocked access to a Canadian-based Internet service provider after a Canadian student opened a page carrying North Korean propaganda. It lifted the restriction after the page was closed.
